narrative:
The model predicted a 64% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score of 22 was by far the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction heavily toward failure. Compared with an average of 37 among accepted students, this score signaled a much higher risk of struggling with the exam.

Your family income bracket came next. Being in the upper-middle income group actually worked slightly in your favor, nudging the prediction a little toward passing. However, this positive effect was too small to offset the other factors.

Your first-year law school grades (decile 3 out of 10) ranked third. This was below the average of 6 among accepted students and therefore pushed the outcome modestly toward failure.

Taken together, the low LSAT score dominated the model’s thinking, making success look unlikely despite your solid family background.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas you can still change. Retake the LSAT and aim for a substantially higher score. Consider a structured prep course, and if possible, gain additional academic experience that demonstrates improvement before reapplying. This would directly address the factor that weighed most heavily against you.
